344.title: Three turns, twelve aspects
344.hook: each truth known, its task known, its task done: three turns of four truths (SN 56.11)
344.howItsDone: The first sermon, with its three turns and twelve aspects, is chanted in Pali in Theravada monasteries, especially on Asalha Puja, and teachers in many schools use the twelve as a map of practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: to be developed, and your line, walk it. Did you take one step on the factor you chose? Today, the four truths and their tasks fit together into one shape. Day three hundred forty-four.

A pilot doesn't take off because she's read about flying. There's a checklist, and every item gets three looks. Do I know what this is? Do I know what I'm supposed to do with it? Have I actually done it? Only when every line has all three ticks does the plane leave the ground. Near the end of his first sermon, the Buddha describes his own checklist, the one he ran through before he would say he was awakened. Four truths, three looks each. Today, the three turns and the twelve aspects.
screen: `A PILOT'S CHECKLIST.` → `THREE LOOKS AT EVERY LINE.` → `THE BUDDHA'S OWN CHECKLIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape. For each of the four truths, the Buddha says three kinds of knowing arose in him. The first turn: this is the truth. This is dukkha. The second turn: this is what's to be done with it. Dukkha is to be understood. The third turn: it has been done. Dukkha has been understood. Then the same three for the cause: this is the arising; it's to be let go; it has been let go. For the ending: this is the ending; it's to be realized; it has been realized. For the path: this is the path; it's to be developed; it has been developed. Four truths times three turns: twelve aspects. And then the striking line. The Buddha tells the five monks that as long as his knowledge of these three turns and twelve aspects wasn't fully clear, he didn't claim to be awakened. Only when all twelve were clear did he say it. That's honesty about his own path, built right into the first sermon. Then the story turns. As the sermon ends, one of the five, Kondañña, sees it. The sutta says the clear vision arose in him that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease. And the Buddha says, Kondañña has understood. Ever since, he's been known as Añña Kondañña, Kondañña who understood. The sutta says the gods of the earth shouted that the wheel had been set rolling, and the cry passed up through the heavens. Teachers today often use the twelve as a map: knowing a truth, knowing its task, and doing it are three different things.
screen: `THIS IS. TO BE DONE. DONE.` · `FOUR TIMES THREE: TWELVE.` · `NO CLAIM UNTIL ALL TWELVE.` · `KONDAÑÑA UNDERSTOOD.` · then, large: `THREE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to write out the twelve. If you have paper, draw a grid: four rows for the four truths, three columns, this is, to be done, done. Fill in the first two columns as you breathe. Leave the third column empty, or put a light mark where you've had even a small taste. If you have no paper, walk the grid in your mind, one box per breath. No grading. Just the shape. The bell holds the time.
Three turns. Each of the four truths known three ways: this is it, this is what's to be done, it has been done. Twelve aspects in all.
Your line: three turns. Today, pick one thing you know you should do, and notice which turn you're on: knowing it, knowing what to do, or having done it. Day three hundred forty-four.

match.prompt: match each turn to what it says.
pairs: this is what's to be done
the first of the five to understand

myth: the Buddha says he claimed awakening before all twelve aspects were clear
he says he didn't claim it until all three turns of all four truths were fully clear.
four truths times three turns makes twelve aspects
this is it, it's to be done, it has been done, for each of the four.
Kondañña's name came to mean Kondañña who understood
the Buddha said Kondañña has understood, and the name stuck.

fork.setup: the sermon ends. one of the five listeners has seen it. what does the sutta say he saw?
options: that the Buddha was a god.
that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease.
that the world will end soon.
fork.reveal: Kondañña saw that whatever arises is subject to ceasing, and the Buddha said: Kondañña has understood.

original.note: Pali tiparivaṭṭa: three turns or rounds; the first sermon's three turns of knowing for each truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowing the four truths means being able to list them.
what it means: each truth is known three ways: as true, as a task, and as a task done.
what a scholar hears: SN 56.11 calls this tiparivaṭṭa dvādasākāra, three turns and twelve aspects, and only then has the Buddha claim anuttara sammāsambodhi.

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the three turns and twelve aspects; Kondañña's insight

345.title: A handful of leaves
345.hook: the Buddha holds a few leaves: what I have taught is this; what I know is the forest; I taught what helps (SN 56.31)
345.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of the simsapa leaves to explain why the teaching centers on the four noble truths and on what leads to peace, rather than on every question that can be asked.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three turns, and your line, three turns. Did you notice which turn you were on with one thing: knowing it, knowing what to do, or having done it? Day three hundred forty-five.

Ask a great cook for her recipe and she'll often give you five ingredients. Not because she only knows five things. She knows the history of the dish, the chemistry of the onion, the story of the aunt who taught her. She leaves all that out on purpose, because you need to make dinner tonight. You heard the story of the handful of leaves on the last day of year one, as a lookout over the road ahead. Today it comes back where it belongs in the Connected Discourses, right after the four truths, and this time we'll listen for the reasons.
screen: `A GREAT COOK'S FIVE INGREDIENTS.` → `SHE LEAVES THE REST OUT.` → `LISTEN FOR THE REASONS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi. He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, these in my hand or the leaves in the grove overhead? The leaves in the grove, they say, by far. In the same way, he says, the things I have directly known but not taught are far more. Then comes the part that's easy to skip. Why hasn't he taught them? Because, he says, they aren't beneficial. They don't belong to the basics of the holy life. They don't lead to letting go, to calm, to peace, to direct knowing, to awakening, to nibbana. And what has he taught? This is dukkha. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Why? Because that does help. It leads to letting go, to calm, to peace, to awakening. So the handful isn't a random sample. It's a careful choice, and the filter is simple: does it help? Notice that the Buddha isn't hiding anything mysterious behind his back, or saying the rest of the forest is forbidden. He's being a teacher who knows what a student needs, the way the cook knows you need dinner. That's why this sutta sits in the book of the four truths. It's the Buddha explaining why the last two weeks have been about four sentences and not four hundred. And it hands us a test we can use on anything we read, watch, or worry about: does this lead to calm and freedom, or just to more noise?
screen: `WHICH ARE MORE?` · `WHY NOT THE FOREST?` · `WHAT'S IN THE HAND.` · `THE FILTER: DOES IT HELP?` · then, large: `ONLY WHAT HELPS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hold a handful of leaves. If you can, pick up a few real leaves from outside, or anything small: a few coins, some dried beans. Hold them loosely in your open palm. Feel their weight, and how little it is. Then, breathing slowly, let your mind fill with everything you're carrying today: plans, news, worries. For each one, ask quietly: is this in the handful, or is it the forest? Let the forest go. The bell holds the time.
A handful of leaves. What the Buddha taught, compared to what he knew: a small handful, chosen because it helps toward peace and freedom.
Your line: only what helps. Today, before you open one more tab or start one more worry, ask the Buddha's question: does this help? If not, leave it in the forest. Day three hundred forty-five.

pairs: what he knew but didn't teach

he left them out because they don't help toward letting go, peace and awakening.
the handful the Buddha taught is the four noble truths
dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way.
the story takes place in a simsapa grove near Kosambi
that's the setting the sutta gives.

fork.setup: you're a monk in the simsapa grove. the Buddha says he knows far more than he's taught. why, he asks, hasn't he taught it?
options: because you aren't ready for secrets.
because it doesn't help toward peace and awakening.
because he forgot it.
fork.reveal: he says the rest isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to letting go, calm, peace and nibbana; the four truths do.

original.note: Pali siṃsapā: the simsapa tree (often identified as Indian rosewood), whose grove gives the sutta its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the handful of leaves means the Buddha kept secrets.
what it means: he chose to teach only what helps toward freedom, and named it: the four truths.

what a scholar hears: SN 56.31 sits in the Saccasaṃyutta, the connected sayings on the truths; its list, nibbidā, virāga, nirodha, upasama, abhiññā, sambodhi, nibbāna, recurs across the canon as the test of what is worth teaching.

sources.ref: SN 56.31 (Simsapa Sutta, the handful of leaves)

346.title: The poisoned arrow
346.hook: a wounded man refuses treatment until he knows who shot him and why (MN 63)
346.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set certain metaphysical questions aside and focused on the four truths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a handful of leaves, and your line, only what helps. Did you leave one worry in the forest? Today, a monk who wanted the whole forest. Day three hundred forty-six.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF LEAVES — ONLY WHAT HELPS.`

segments.voice: A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone, and he's annoyed. There are questions the Buddha has never answered. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or finite? Is the soul the same as the body, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither? He makes up his mind. He'll go to the Buddha and demand answers. And if the Buddha won't give them, he'll give up the robe and go back to ordinary life. It's an ultimatum. The Buddha answers it with a story about an arrow.
screen: `A MONK, ANNOYED.` → `TEN BIG QUESTIONS.` → `ANSWER, OR I LEAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha asks him: did I ever say, come and live the holy life and I'll answer these for you? No, Malunkyaputta admits. Did you ever say, I'll live it only if you answer? No. Then the story. A man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: I won't let this arrow be pulled out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What's his name, his clan? Was he tall or short? Dark or golden-skinned? What village is he from? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow? What was the bowstring made of? The shaft? Which bird's feathers were on it? The Buddha says simply: that man would die, and still not know. Then he explains. Whether the world is eternal or not, there is still birth, aging, death, sorrow and grief, and their ending is what he teaches. He left those ten questions undeclared, he says, because answering them isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to peace and awakening. What he has declared: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. Two things worth noticing. The Buddha doesn't say the questions are stupid, or forbidden to think about. He says they're not the urgent thing. And the story is told with real humor: the list of questions about feathers and bowstrings goes on and on, until you can almost hear the monks laughing. Everyone has an arrow somewhere. And everyone has a list of questions they'd like answered before dealing with it.
screen: `DID I EVER PROMISE ANSWERS?` · `WHO SHOT ME? WHAT FEATHERS?` · `HE'D DIE STILL ASKING.` · `UNDECLARED, NOT FORBIDDEN.` · then, large: `PULL THE ARROW OUT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to drop one idle question. Sit and breathe. Notice a question your mind has been circling: why did they say that, what will happen next year, what does that look mean. Ask honestly: does answering this help with what hurts right now? If not, set it down for these few minutes. Then turn gently toward the arrow itself, whatever is actually stinging, and simply feel it with care. The bell holds the time.
The poisoned arrow. The Buddha's story of a wounded man who wants every answer before treatment: the urgent thing is the arrow, not the archer.
Your line: pull the arrow out. Today, when you catch yourself asking who's to blame for a hurt, ask instead what would help it, and do that first. Day three hundred forty-six.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the arrow story.
pairs: wanted to know about the archer

myth: the Buddha said the ten questions were forbidden to think about
he left them undeclared because answering them doesn't lead to peace and awakening.
the Buddha never promised Malunkyaputta answers to those questions
he asks, and Malunkyaputta admits no such promise was made.
in the story the man asks even what feathers were on the arrow
the list runs from the archer's clan down to the bowstring and feathers.

fork.setup: you've been shot with a poisoned arrow. the surgeon is here. what do you do?
options: let the surgeon pull it out.
first find out who shot you.
first find out what the bowstring was made of.
fork.reveal: the man in the story insists on knowing everything first, and the Buddha says he'd die still not knowing; the arrow comes first.

original.note: Pali salla: a dart or arrow; the Buddha is called sallakatta, the remover of arrows, a surgeon.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha dodged hard questions.
what it means: he set them aside on purpose, because they don't help end suffering, and named what does.

what a scholar hears: MN 63 lists ten avyākata, undeclared points, on the world, the soul and the Tathāgata after death; whether the Buddha held them unanswerable or merely unhelpful is still discussed by scholars.

347.title: The blind turtle
347.hook: a turtle surfacing once a century through a yoke adrift on the ocean: human birth is that rare (SN 56.48)
347.howItsDone: Many Buddhists, especially in Tibetan traditions, reflect on the precious human life at the start of practice, often recalling the image of the blind turtle and the yoke.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the poisoned arrow, and your line, pull the arrow out. Did you ask what would help a hurt before asking who caused it? Day three hundred forty-seven.
screen: `THE POISONED ARROW — PULL THE ARROW OUT.`

segments.voice: The odds of a particular person being born are hard to even write down. Your parents had to meet, on that day, and their parents before them, back through every war and famine and missed train. People like to play with those numbers. The Buddha played with them too, only he didn't use numbers. He used an ocean, a wooden yoke with a single hole, and a turtle who can't see. It's one of the strangest pictures in the whole canon, and it sits in the book of the four truths for a reason. Today, the blind turtle.
screen: `THE ODDS OF BEING BORN.` → `AN OCEAN, A YOKE, A TURTLE.` → `IN THE BOOK OF THE FOUR TRUTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the picture, from the Connected Discourses. Suppose someone threw a yoke into the great ocean, the wooden collar you'd put on an ox, with a single hole in it. The east wind pushes it west. The west wind pushes it east. The north wind pushes it south, the south wind north. And in that ocean there's a turtle, blind in both eyes, who comes up to the surface once every hundred years. What are the chances, the Buddha asks, that the turtle, coming up, would push its neck through the hole in that drifting yoke? Very slim, the monks say. It might happen only after a very long time. Even so, the Buddha says, it's that hard to be born human. The neighboring sutta enlarges the scene to the whole earth as one ocean. And then the point lands, the reason the turtle is here in the book of the truths. The Buddha says many beings don't see the four truths. So, he concludes, effort should be made to understand: this is dukkha, this is its arising, this is its ending, this is the way. The turtle isn't there to make anyone feel lucky, or anxious. It's there to make this hour feel valuable. Buddhist teachers call it a precious human life: a life with the time, the senses and the freedom to hear the teaching and practice it. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says it plainly: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals." Different schools read rebirth in their own ways. They agree on the urgency.
screen: `A YOKE WITH ONE HOLE.` · `A TURTLE, ONCE A CENTURY.` · `THAT HARD TO BE BORN HUMAN.` · `SO, UNDERSTAND THE FOUR TRUTHS.` · then, large: `RARER THAN THE TURTLE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to value this hour. Sit, and feel that you're here: breathing, hearing, able to think. Picture the wide gray ocean, the yoke drifting, and a turtle rising, just once, into the light. Let that picture be this moment. Breathe in, knowing you have this breath. Breathe out, knowing it won't come again in quite this way. Don't hurry to use the hour well. Just feel what it's worth. The bell holds the time.
The blind turtle. The Buddha's picture of how rare a human birth is: a blind turtle surfacing once a century through a single drifting yoke.
Your line: rarer than the turtle. Today, choose one hour you'd normally waste, and give it to something that matters to you: a person, a practice, a walk. Day three hundred forty-seven.

pairs: one hole, pushed by four winds
a human birth is that rare
make an effort to see the four truths

myth: the turtle story is told to make people feel anxious
it's there to make this hour feel valuable, and to urge the four truths.
the sutta ends by urging effort to understand the four truths
that's why it's in the book of the truths.
the turtle surfaces once every year
once every hundred years, and it's blind.

fork.setup: the Buddha asks: a blind turtle surfaces once a century. what are the odds it puts its neck through a single drifting yoke? what do you say?
options: very likely.
very slim; only after a very long time.
impossible.
fork.reveal: the monks say it might happen only after a very long time; the Buddha says a human birth is that hard to come by.

original.note: Pali kacchapa: a turtle or tortoise; the sutta's blind turtle is kāṇo kacchapo.

trapdoor: what you thought: the blind turtle is about how lucky you are.
what it means: a human life is rare, so use it to understand the four truths.

what a scholar hears: SN 56.47 and 56.48 (Chiggaḷa) both end with the refrain tasmā... yogo karaṇīyo, so effort should be made, applied to the four truths; Tibetan teachers later made the image central to reflection on the precious human birth.

sources.ref: SN 56.47–48 (Chiggala Suttas, the yoke with a hole)

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

348.title: This, because of that
348.hook: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises (SN 12.21)
348.howItsDone: Buddhists study dependent arising as a central teaching in every school; Theravada monastics chant its formula, and Mahayana and Tibetan teachers often present it as the key to understanding emptiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the blind turtle, and your line, rarer than the turtle. Did you give one hour to something that matters? Today, the idea underneath the four truths. Day three hundred forty-eight.
screen: `THE BLIND TURTLE — RARER THAN THE TURTLE.`

segments.voice: You're snappish with someone at dinner. Why? Because you're tired. Why tired? Because you slept badly. Why? Because you were up late answering messages. Why? Because a deadline moved. Why did it move? Because someone else's plan fell through, because of their week, because of theirs. Pull on any single mood and you find a thread, and the thread is attached to other threads, all the way out. The Buddha put this into a formula so short you could fit it on a fortune cookie. Today, the teaching called dependent arising.
screen: `SNAPPISH AT DINNER.` → `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `A THREAD ATTACHED TO THREADS.`

segments.voice: The word is paticcasamuppada. Paticca means depending on, leaning on. Samuppada means arising together. Dependent arising, or dependent origination. In the Connected Discourses, book twelve, the Buddha gives it in four lines: When this is, that comes to be. With the arising of this, that arises. When this is not, that does not come to be. With the ending of this, that ends. That's all. No names, no gods, no story. Just a pattern. Here's why it matters for the last two weeks. The four truths say dukkha has a cause, and that it can end. Dependent arising explains how both are possible. If dukkha just existed on its own, nothing could be done. But it doesn't. It leans on conditions. Change the conditions, and it changes. The third and fourth lines are the hopeful ones: when this is not, that does not come to be. There's a famous moment in the Long Discourses. Ananda tells the Buddha that dependent arising, though they say it's deep, seems perfectly clear to him. The Buddha stops him. Don't say that, Ananda, he says. It is deep, and it looks deep, and because people don't understand it, they get tangled like a ball of string. So two things are true at once. It's simple enough to say over dinner, and deep enough to take a lifetime. Buddhist schools have unfolded it in different ways, some as a chain across lifetimes, some as the way every moment hangs together. The formula sits underneath them all.
screen: `PATICCA: LEANING. SAMUPPADA: ARISING.` · `WHEN THIS IS, THAT COMES TO BE.` · `WHEN THIS IS NOT, THAT IS NOT.` · `DON'T SAY THAT, ANANDA.` · then, large: `THIS, BECAUSE OF THAT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to trace one mood to its causes. Sit and settle. Notice the mood you're in right now, whatever it is: flat, restless, content, tense. Name it. Then ask gently: what is this leaning on? Maybe sleep, food, a conversation, the weather. Follow one thread back a step or two. Don't judge any of it. Then notice that the mood is changing even as you watch, because its conditions are. The bell holds the time.
Paticcasamuppada. Dependent arising: when this is, that comes to be; when this ends, that ends. Nothing stands on its own.
Your line: this, because of that. Today, when a feeling surprises you, ask once what it's leaning on, and notice the thread. Day three hundred forty-eight.

pairs: that does not come to be

myth: dependent arising is a story about the gods creating the world
it's a pattern with no names or gods: when this is, that comes to be.
the Buddha told Ananda that dependent arising is deep
Ananda called it clear, and the Buddha said: don't say that; it is deep.
the formula includes how things end, not only how they arise
when this is not, that does not come to be; with the ending of this, that ends.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. you tell the Buddha that dependent arising, though people call it deep, seems perfectly clear to you. what does he say?
options: well done, you've understood it.
don't say that; it is deep, and people get tangled for not understanding it.

fork.reveal: he stops Ananda: it is deep and looks deep, and not understanding it, people get tangled like a ball of string.

original.note: Pali paṭiccasamuppāda, Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda: dependent arising, things arising in dependence on conditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason.
what it means: everything happens because of conditions, and changes when they change.
what a scholar hears: the formula imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati recurs in SN 12.21 and elsewhere; DN 15 opens with the Buddha correcting Ananda's sense that it is easy.

sources.ref: DN 15 (Mahanidana Sutta), Ananda told not to call it clear

349.title: The twelve links
349.hook: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, aging-and-death (SN 12.1)
349.howItsDone: In Tibetan monasteries the wheel of life is painted near the entrance with the twelve links around its rim; in Theravada lands the links are chanted and studied, often following the commentaries' three-life reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday: paticcasamuppada, and your line, this, because of that. Did you follow one feeling back to what it was leaning on? Today, the pattern spelled out link by link. Day three hundred forty-nine.

On the wall of many Tibetan temples, near the entrance, there's a huge painted wheel held in the claws and teeth of a fierce figure. Around its outer rim run twelve small pictures. A blind person with a stick. A potter at his wheel. A monkey swinging through a tree. People in a boat. A house with windows. A couple embracing. A man with an arrow in his eye. Someone drinking. Someone picking fruit. A pregnant woman. A birth. And an old body being carried away. It looks like a puzzle. It's a teaching. Today, the twelve links of dependent arising.
screen: `A PAINTED WHEEL BY THE DOOR.` → `TWELVE SMALL PICTURES.` → `A PUZZLE THAT'S A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: The very first sutta in the book on dependent arising, in the Connected Discourses, lays the chain out. With ignorance as condition, there are formations. Then the links run on: consciousness; name-and-form, meaning the mind and body together; the six senses; contact, where a sense meets its object; feeling, pleasant, painful or neither; craving; clinging; becoming; birth; and finally aging and death, with sorrow, grief and despair. Such, the sutta says, is the arising of this whole mass of dukkha. Now match them to the wheel. Ignorance is the blind person, feeling the way. Formations, the potter shaping pots, the way past actions shape what comes. Consciousness is the monkey, jumping from branch to branch. Name-and-form, the people in the boat, traveling together. The six senses, the house with its windows. Contact, the embrace. Feeling, the arrow in the eye. Craving is drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit, becoming is the pregnancy, then birth, then the body carried off. The paintings are a later Indian and Tibetan tradition; the suttas give only the list. There's also the second half of that same sutta, which runs the chain backward: with the ending of ignorance, formations end, and so on, link by link, to the ending of this whole mass of dukkha. How to read the chain is something Buddhists have discussed for centuries. The Theravada commentaries often spread it across three lifetimes: past, present and future. Many teachers also read it moment by moment, in a single afternoon. Both readings are part of the living tradition.
screen: `WITH IGNORANCE AS CONDITION.` · `TWELVE LINKS, ONE BY ONE.` · `THE BLIND ONE, THE POTTER, THE MONKEY.` · `ACROSS LIVES, OR IN A MOMENT.` · then, large: `TWELVE LINKS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to learn the twelve links. Sit, and on each breath name one link, and let its picture appear. Ignorance: the blind one. Formations: the potter. Consciousness: the monkey. Name-and-form: the boat. Six senses: the house. Contact: the embrace. Feeling: the arrow. Craving: drinking. Clinging: grabbing fruit. Becoming: the pregnancy. Birth. Aging and death. Then go around again, slower. If you lose your place, start at the blind one. The bell holds the time.
The twelve links. Dependent arising spelled out: from ignorance to aging and death, each link leaning on the one before, and each one able to end.
Your line: twelve links. Today, try to say all twelve once from memory, on a walk or while you wait for something. Notice which links you forget. Day three hundred forty-nine.

pairs: a blind person with a stick
a monkey swinging through a tree
a man with an arrow in his eye

the suttas give the list; the paintings are a later Indian and Tibetan tradition.
the same sutta also runs the chain toward its ending
with the ending of ignorance, formations end, and so on to the end of this mass of dukkha.
all Buddhists read the chain only across three lifetimes
the commentaries often do; many teachers also read it moment by moment.

fork.setup: you're looking at the wheel of life. you spot a monkey swinging from branch to branch. which link is it?
options: craving.
consciousness.
clinging.
fork.reveal: the monkey is consciousness, jumping from one object to the next; craving is someone drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit nidāna: a cause or source, the usual word for each of the twelve links.

trapdoor: what you thought: the twelve links are a list to memorize.
what it means: they show how dukkha arises one condition at a time, and how it ends the same way.

what a scholar hears: SN 12.1 opens the Nidānasaṃyutta with both the arising and the cessation sequence; Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga XVII sets out the three-life reading, while other teachers apply the links to a single moment.

sources.ref: SN 12.1 (Paticcasamuppada Sutta), the twelve links forward and in reverse
Visuddhimagga XVII (dependent origination across three lives)

350.title: Where the chain breaks
350.hook: between feeling and craving there is a gap where the chain can be cut
350.howItsDone: In many Buddhist meditation traditions, practitioners note feelings as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral as they arise, so that craving and aversion can be seen before they take hold.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the twelve links, and your line, twelve links. Could you say all twelve from memory? Which one slipped away? Today ends the week, and we look for the weak link. Day three hundred fifty.

Someone cuts in front of you in line. There's a hot flash of unpleasantness, right in the chest. That part is quick and nobody chose it. And then, in less time than it takes to blink, the second part arrives: the story, the glare, the rehearsed speech, the replay on the drive home. Most days, those two parts feel like one event. They aren't. Between them there's a seam. Buddhist teachers have pointed at that seam for centuries, because on the wheel of twelve links, it's where the chain is thinnest. Today, where the chain breaks.
screen: `SOMEONE CUTS IN LINE.` → `A HOT FLASH. THEN THE STORY.` → `BETWEEN THEM, A SEAM.`

segments.voice: Look at the middle of the chain. Contact gives rise to feeling: pleasant, painful or neither. Feeling gives rise to craving: want more, want it gone. The suttas don't use the word gap. That image comes from how many teachers apply the links. But the suttas do say this: an awakened person still feels. Still has a body, still meets heat and cold and rude people. What doesn't follow is the craving. So the link from feeling to craving isn't welded. Here's how the Buddha pictured it, in a sutta called the Arrow, in the Connected Discourses. When an untrained person is touched by a painful feeling, he grieves and laments and gets confused. He feels two pains, one in the body and one in the mind, like a man shot with one arrow and then shot again with a second. The trained person feels the first arrow and isn't hit by the second. The first arrow is feeling. The second is everything we pile on top. That's the seam, and it's where practice works. Not by refusing to feel, but by meeting the feeling cleanly, so craving has nothing to grab. Now the week, from the top. Three turns: each truth known, its task known, its task done. A handful of leaves: only what helps. The poisoned arrow: treat the wound before asking who shot it. The blind turtle: a rare human life. This, because of that: dependent arising in four lines. The twelve links, on the painted wheel. And today, the place to cut.
screen: `FEELING, THEN CRAVING.` · `THE AWAKENED STILL FEEL.` · `THE FIRST ARROW AND THE SECOND.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `CUT BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to catch one feeling before the craving. Sit still, and wait. Sooner or later something will happen: an itch, a sound, an ache, a pleasant warmth. The moment you notice it, label it softly: pleasant, or unpleasant, or neither. That's the first arrow. Then watch, with real curiosity, for the next half-second, the lean toward or away. If you see it, you've found the seam. Don't fight the lean. Just see it. The bell holds the time.
Where the chain breaks. Between feeling and craving: the first arrow comes, and the second doesn't have to.
Your line: cut between. Today, when something stings, say to yourself: first arrow. Then see if you can skip the second, just once. Day three hundred fifty.

match.prompt: match each piece to today's teaching.
pairs: the grief and story piled on

myth: the suttas use the exact word gap for this point in the chain
the image comes from how teachers apply the links; the suttas show feeling without craving.
in the Arrow sutta, the trained person still feels bodily pain
he feels the first arrow and isn't hit by the second.
cutting the chain means refusing to feel anything
it means meeting the feeling cleanly, so craving has nothing to grab.

fork.setup: you stub your toe hard. by the Arrow sutta, what can training change?
options: the pain in the toe.
the second arrow: the grief, story and anger on top.
nothing at all.
fork.reveal: the trained person still feels the first arrow, the bodily pain, but isn't struck by the second.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit vedanā: feeling, the felt tone of pleasant, painful or neither, the link just before craving.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you feel pain, you're bound to suffer.
what it means: feeling comes, but craving and the second arrow don't have to follow.

what a scholar hears: in the twelve links vedanā-paccayā taṇhā, feeling conditions craving; SN 36.6 (Sallatha) and the suttas' accounts of arahants still feeling show the condition need not produce the result.

sources.ref: SN 12.1 (the twelve links: feeling conditions craving)
